a: Permissible due to length of verse, but continuing is better

q: Which waqf mark means: 'Permissible due to length of verse, but continuing is better...'?
What does the waqf mark 'قف' (Waqf Awla) mean?
a: Stopping is preferred — better to stop than to continue here
wrong: Stopping and continuing are exactly equal

q: Which waqf mark means: 'Stopping is preferred — better to stop than to continue here...'?
What does the waqf mark '...' (Waqf Mu'anaqah) mean?
a: Stop at one set of dots or the other, not both — the meanings are linked between them
wrong: Never stop at any of the markers
Mandatory stop at the first marker only

q: Which waqf mark means: 'Stop at one set of dots or the other, not both — the meanings are link...'?
What does the waqf mark 'صل' (Wasl Awla) mean?
a: Continuing without stopping is preferred — do not stop if possible
wrong: Stopping and continuing are equally fine

q: Which waqf mark means: 'Continuing without stopping is preferred — do not stop if possible...'?
What does the waqf mark 'وقفة' (Waqfah) mean?
a: A brief pause without a full stop — do not take a new breath

q: Which waqf mark means: 'A brief pause without a full stop — do not take a new breath...'?

hadith: Actions are judged by intentions, and every person will have only what they intended. Whoever migrates for Allah and His Messenger, his migration is for Allah and His Messenger. Whoever migrates for worldly gain or to marry a woman, his migration is for that.
q: What does this hadith teach about deeds done outwardly the same way?
a: Two people doing the same action may receive completely different rewards based on their intention
wrong: The action itself determines the reward regardless of intent
Only deeds of worship require intention
Intention only matters for acts of charity

hadith: One day while we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah, a man appeared — his clothes were very white, his hair very black, with no signs of travel, yet none of us knew him. He sat with the Prophet and asked about Islam, Iman, and Ihsan. The Prophet replied: Islam is the five pillars. Iman is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree. Ihsan is to worship Allah as though you see Him; if you cannot, then know that He sees you.
q: What is Ihsan according to this hadith?
a: Worshipping Allah as though you see Him — and if you cannot, knowing He sees you
wrong: Believing in the six pillars of faith
Giving charity openly to inspire others

hadith: Islam is built on five things: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger, establishing prayer, giving zakat, fasting Ramadan, and making Hajj to the House for those who are able.
q: What does this hadith clarify about Hajj?
a: Hajj is only obligatory for those who are able — it is conditional, unlike the other pillars
wrong: Hajj must be done every year
Hajj replaces zakat for those who perform it
Hajj is optional for all Muslims

hadith: Each of you is brought together in your mother's womb for forty days as a drop, then is a clot for a like period, then a morsel for a like period. Then an angel is sent and breathes the soul into it, and is commanded to write four things: the person's provision, their lifespan, their deeds, and whether they will be wretched or happy.
q: What theological lesson comes from the angel writing 'wretched or happy' before birth?
a: Allah's knowledge of our fate is complete before we exist, yet we are still responsible for our choices
wrong: Our fate is sealed and our actions have no meaning
Only good deeds can change what was written
The soul entering the body erases the written decree

hadith: Whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not of it will have it rejected.
q: What is this hadith the primary evidence for in Islamic jurisprudence?
a: The prohibition of bid'ah — religious innovations not grounded in the Quran and Sunnah
wrong: The permissibility of local customs in worship
The requirement to consult the community before new rulings

hadith: The halal is clear and the haram is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that most people do not know about. Whoever avoids doubtful matters has protected his religion and honour. Whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into haram, like a shepherd who grazes near a sanctuary — he is likely to enter it. Every king has a sanctuary, and Allah's sanctuary is His prohibitions.
q: What does the shepherd analogy teach in this hadith?
a: Getting close to what is forbidden — even in grey areas — puts you at risk of crossing the boundary
wrong: A shepherd must protect his flock from all water sources
Halal and haram are only clear to scholars
Doubtful matters are always permissible if unsure

hadith: The religion is sincerity (nasihah). We said: To whom? He said: To Allah, to His book, to His messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims, and to the common people.
q: Why is 'sincerity to the common people' included in this hadith?
a: Nasihah to laypeople means genuinely guiding, advising, and caring for all Muslims — not just leadership
wrong: Common people must follow leaders without question
Sincerity only applies to those in authority
The hadith only refers to sincerity in acts of worship

hadith: Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not make people run away.
q: What approach to teaching and leadership does this hadith encourage?
a: Facilitating understanding and encouraging people rather than burdening or alienating them
wrong: Strict enforcement of all rules at all times
Only scholars should speak to the public
Hiding difficult rulings from new Muslims

hadith: Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is leaving what does not concern him.
q: What is a sign of spiritual maturity according to this hadith?
a: Focusing only on what benefits you and avoiding unnecessary involvement in others' affairs
wrong: Advising everyone around you on all matters
Maximising your knowledge of every topic
Speaking frequently so your voice is heard

hadith: Allah is pure and accepts only what is pure. He commanded the believers as He commanded the messengers. A man travels, his hair dishevelled and dusty, raising his hands to the sky: 'O Lord! O Lord!' — yet his food is haram, his drink is haram, his clothing is haram, his nourishment is haram. How can he be answered?
q: What barrier to having du'a answered does this hadith highlight?
a: Consuming haram wealth or food blocks the acceptance of supplication, regardless of sincerity
wrong: Du'a is never answered without completing Hajj
Du'a must be made in Arabic to be answered

hadith: Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt, for truthfulness is tranquility and lying is doubt.
q: What inner tool does this hadith give for navigating unclear situations?
a: Your sense of inner peace and discomfort — peace indicates righteousness, unease indicates sin
wrong: Always ask a scholar before acting
Doubt always means something is haram
Ignore feelings and follow legal opinions only

hadith: None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
q: What standard of brotherhood does this hadith establish?
a: Genuine faith requires actively wishing for others the same good you desire for yourself
wrong: Brotherhood only applies to people of the same family
It is enough to not harm others to fulfill this
This applies only to acts of charity and money

hadith: The blood of a Muslim is not lawful to shed except in three cases: the previously married adulterer, a life for a life, and the one who abandons his religion and separates from the community.
q: What does this hadith establish about human life in Islam?
a: The sanctity of Muslim life is a foundational principle — taking it is only permitted in the most serious cases and only by proper authority
wrong: Anyone can enforce these three cases
The list is not exhaustive and scholars can add cases
Apostasy alone is always punishable by death in all circumstances

hadith: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest.
q: What does linking these behaviours to belief in Allah and the Last Day imply?
a: These social duties are not merely cultural — they are expressions of faith and will be accounted for
wrong: Good speech only applies in formal settings
Neighbours are only those directly next door
Guests must be hosted for exactly three days no more

hadith: Do not be angry. The Prophet repeated this three times.
q: Why is controlling anger so significant that the Prophet emphasised it three times?
a: Anger is a root cause of many sins — controlling it protects relationships, judgment, and one's deen
wrong: The Prophet repeated it because the companion was hard of hearing
Anger is only prohibited during prayer
The repetition is a literary style with no added emphasis

hadith: Allah prescribed excellence (ihsan) in all things. So if you kill, kill well; if you slaughter, slaughter well; sharpen your blade and spare your animal the agony.
q: What broad principle does this hadith establish beyond just slaughter?
a: Excellence (ihsan) is an Islamic value in every act — even difficult or terminal ones must be done with care and competence
wrong: Only acts of worship require perfection
This ruling only applies to professional butchers
The hadith permits any method as long as the animal dies

hadith: Fear Allah wherever you are. Follow a bad deed with a good one to erase it. And treat people with good character.
q: What practical tool for managing sin does this hadith provide?
a: Following a sin immediately with a good deed — tawbah expressed through action — as a way to erase its effect
wrong: Only formal repentance through prayer removes sin
Good deeds before a sin cancel its effect
You must confess sins to a scholar to erase them

hadith: Be mindful of Allah and He will protect you. Be mindful of Allah and you will find Him before you. Know Him in times of ease and He will know you in times of hardship. When you ask, ask Allah. When you seek help, seek it from Allah.
q: What relationship dynamic does 'know Allah in ease and He will know you in hardship' describe?
a: Building a relationship with Allah during good times creates a foundation He responds to in difficulty
wrong: Allah only responds to those in crisis regardless of past deeds
Du'a is more powerful when made in hardship than in ease
Knowing Allah means memorising His 99 names

hadith: If you do what pleases people but angers Allah, He will give you over to the people. But if you do what pleases Allah though it angers people, Allah will protect you from the people.
q: What does this hadith warn about people-pleasing at the expense of Allah's pleasure?
a: Prioritising people's approval over Allah's leads to dependence on people — and losing both Allah's support and theirs
wrong: It is always necessary to balance pleasing Allah and people equally
Social harmony is always more important than strict rulings
This only applies to scholars not laypeople

hadith: If you feel no shame, then do as you wish.
q: What role does hayaa (modesty/shame) play in Islamic morality according to this hadith?
a: Hayaa is an internal moral compass — its absence removes the barrier between a person and any sin
wrong: Shame is only relevant in public settings
The hadith gives permission to do anything you like
Modesty only applies to dress and physical appearance

hadith: Say: I believe in Allah — then be steadfast.
q: What does 'be steadfast' add to simply saying 'I believe'?
a: Belief must be lived consistently over time — istiqamah (steadfastness) is what separates conviction from claim
wrong: Steadfastness only applies to the five pillars
The statement of belief alone is sufficient for salvation
Istiqamah means never making mistakes in worship

hadith: There should be no harming and no reciprocating harm.
q: What legal principle in Islamic fiqh does this short hadith establish?
a: The removal of harm (dar' al-mafsada) is a foundational legal maxim — harm cannot be repaid with harm
wrong: Retaliation in equal measure is always permitted
This only applies to physical injury between Muslims
The hadith overrides the qisas principle completely

hadith: Allah said: O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not oppress one another. Every one of you is astray except those I have guided, so seek guidance from Me. Every one of you is hungry except those I have fed, so seek food from Me.
q: What does Allah forbidding injustice for Himself (in a Hadith Qudsi) mean theologically?
a: It emphasises that Allah's prohibition of injustice is absolute and self-willed — not imposed — making it the highest moral standard
wrong: Allah can commit injustice but chooses not to in most cases
This only applies to physical harm between people
The Hadith Qudsi carries less authority than regular hadith

hadith: Part of the perfection of one's Islam is leaving what does not concern him.
q: How does this relate to social media and information overload in a modern context?
a: Consuming and reacting to everything that doesn't benefit you is a failure of spiritual discipline — restraint is a sign of mature faith
wrong: Muslims must stay informed about all world events
This hadith only applies to private conversations
Leaving things that don't concern you applies only to gossip

hadith: On every joint of a person there is a charitable act due every day the sun rises: mediating between two people is charity; helping someone load his mount is charity; a good word is charity; every step taken toward prayer is charity; removing harm from the path is charity.
q: What does this hadith teach about the scope of Islamic charity?
a: Sadaqa is not limited to money — every beneficial act for others or society counts as charity
wrong: Only financial giving counts as sadaqa
Sadaqa is only for the poor and needy
This type of charity only applies during Ramadan

hadith: Righteousness is good character, and sin is what disturbs the soul and you dislike people knowing about it.
q: What internal test for sin does this hadith offer?
a: If an action unsettles your conscience and you would be ashamed if others saw it — that discomfort is itself a sign of sin
wrong: Public opinion determines what is sinful
Only scholars can define what sin is
The heart is not a reliable guide — only text defines sin

hadith: Whoever relieves a believer of a worldly hardship, Allah will relieve him of a hardship on the Day of Judgment. Whoever makes things easy for one in difficulty, Allah will ease his situation in this world and the next. Whoever conceals a Muslim's faults, Allah will conceal his faults in this world and the next.
q: What pattern does Allah's response follow in this hadith?
a: Allah mirrors the nature of the deed — ease given creates ease received; concealment given creates concealment received
wrong: Rewards are only given in the Hereafter not in this world
Only helping in financial matters earns this reward
The reward is based on the amount of effort not the type of deed

hadith: I urge you to follow my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly-guided caliphs after me. Hold fast to it and bite onto it with your molar teeth. Beware of newly invented matters, for every new matter is an innovation, and every innovation is going astray.
q: Why does the Prophet say 'bite onto it with your molar teeth'?
a: It conveys that holding onto the Sunnah requires fierce determination — it will not be easy and people will try to pull you away
wrong: It is a literal instruction about how to eat during worship
The phrase refers to keeping the tongue from speaking falsehood
Molar teeth are symbolic of scholars who preserve the deen

hadith: Verily Allah has obligated certain duties, so do not neglect them. He has set certain limits, so do not transgress them. He has prohibited certain things, so do not violate them. And He has been silent about certain things — out of mercy for you, not forgetfulness — so do not seek them out.
q: What does 'He has been silent about certain things out of mercy' mean?
a: Matters not addressed explicitly are a mercy — adding rulings where silence exists is a burden Allah did not intend
wrong: Scholars must fill in all silences with rulings
Silent matters are always considered forbidden
The Sunnah provides rulings for every possible situation

hadith: Take advantage of five before five: your youth before old age, your health before sickness, your wealth before poverty, your free time before being occupied, and your life before death.
q: Why does this hadith list these five in this particular order?
a: They move from the most taken-for-granted to the most obvious — we recognise the value of life only at death, but waste youth, health, and time first
wrong: The order reflects the five pillars of Islam
The hadith ranks these by religious obligation
Youth comes first because it is the only one fully in our control
